title: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
hookLine: on that day each flees mother, father, wife and children (80:34–37)

lines: WHEN THE WORST HAPPENS, FAMILY RUNS TOWARD.
A DAY IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY.
cards: A crowded family photo. Grandparents in the middle, cousins squeezed in at the edges, someone's kid making a face. When the worst happens, these are the people a family runs toward, not away.

The end of 'Abasa describes a day when that instinct runs the other way. It's an unsettling image, and commentators don't read it as fear for its own sake. It says something about today, while the photo is still full.

teach.b: Verse thirty-three: when the deafening blast comes. The word is as-sakhkhah, which commentators explain as a sound so loud it strikes the ears.

Then verse thirty-four, in Pickthall's words: On the day when a man fleeth from his brother. The list goes on: and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children. Commentators notice the order.
It moves inward: a brother, the parents who raised you, the spouse beside you, your own children, the closest of all. The closest circle of a life, one ring at a time, and each one fled. Why?
Verse thirty-seven: every one of them, that day, will have concern enough of his own. Not cruelty. Overwhelm.
Each person alone with their own record, as At-Takwir put it: a soul will know what it has brought. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim adds a human moment.
Aisha heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ describe people raised on that day, and asked: wouldn't they look at one another?
He answered that the matter would be too serious for that. In one version, in Tirmidhi, he recited verse thirty-seven. Then the surah ends with faces, as Al-Ghashiyah did.
Some bright, laughing, rejoicing. Some covered in dust. So what is it for?
Some readers hear it not as a reason to fear family, but the opposite.
That day, each is alone. Today, no one has to be. The brother can still be called, the mother visited, the child held.
Read that way, the verse makes the present precious, because it won't always be like this.

how: Muslims read the end of 'Abasa as a description of the Day of Resurrection, and some take it as a reason to keep family ties, silat al-rahim, strong now, visiting parents and relatives and mending quarrels.

o: he laughed, glad at what he heard
he frowned, the surah's first word
he wept, mourning what he lost

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: the list of people fled moves from the closest outward
it moves inward: brother, then parents, then spouse, then children.
Aisha asked the Prophet whether people would look at one another that day
a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim: the matter would be too serious to look at one another.
the verse is meant to make people distant from their families now
read one way, it makes today precious: that day each is alone; today no one has to be.

games.q: on that day, a man flees his brother, his parents, his wife and his children. why, according to verse 37?
o: each has concern enough of his own
games.why: every one of them, that day, will have concern enough of his own (80:37). not cruelty: overwhelm.

practice: Picture the people closest to you, one ring at a time: a sibling or a friend like one, your parents or whoever raised you, a partner, children if you have them, or the young people you love.
Let each face come clearly; today they are all within reach. Rest on the one you'd most like to hold close today, a call, a visit, a long hug.

wordCard.voice: 'Abasa. He frowned, Surah eighty, which ends with a day when each person flees even the people closest to them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "he flees," from f-r-r, to run away (Qur'an 80:34).

carryVoice: Your line: each alone that day. And today, the photo is still full. See you tomorrow.
